S1:
The ten payments, all owned in Treasuries from January 2028, fail only if one is short, or late, on its 1 January. A US default could do that – the IPS's own condition. So could a 2028 deposit that never comes, or comes far smaller (Section 2). We name that deposit because it's paid from advances, speaking fees and licences on contract dates – the money a downturn delays first. No fall in share prices can.

A figure Laura has stated fails if the Treasuries behind it pay less, or late, and then it's her word that breaks. Fund costs beyond the fees could, but only by eating through the room under it – about 2% of what the late-2032 fund pays, even with cash waiting earning nothing.

Her flexibility is a limit, not a promise: it can run out without breaking anything she has stated. What would really stretch it is a share slump before the meetings, then a jump in costs. If shares earn the return assumed, her flexibility and what the fund pays above the top cover a rise of about 25% in the US-dollar cost of her share of the building; the worst two-year spans since 1991 rose by more.

The case's fifth area, inflation, decides only what the fixed payments buy, never whether they're paid.

The IPS's two reasons to change the plan – a missed deposit, a Treasury default – are exits for when the plan can't be carried out, not ways a promise fails.
S2:
Laura's ten payments fail if one arrives short, or late, on 1 January. A US default could break them; the IPS says as much. So could a 2028 deposit that never arrives, or arrives far smaller (Section 2). It's the risk we'd point to first: advances, speaking fees and licences are paid on contract dates, and a recession pushes those back. No fall in share prices can. Put the shares at zero – rub out every pencil line, since from January 2028 they're the only pencil left – and the page still reads, all ten payments made.

A stated figure fails if the Treasuries she owns for it pay less, or late, and it's her word that breaks. Fund costs beyond the fees could do it, but only past the room under the figure – about 2% of what the late-2032 fund pays, even if cash waiting earns nothing.

Her flexibility is a limit, so running dry breaks nothing promised. Its weak spot is a share slump before the meetings followed by a cost jump. At the assumed return, her flexibility plus what the fund pays above the top would cover a rise of about 25% in the US-dollar cost of her share of the building, though the worst two-year spans since 1991 rose further.

The case's fifth area, inflation, changes what the fixed payments buy, not whether they arrive.

The IPS's two reasons to change course, a missed deposit and a Treasury default, are exits for when the plan can't go on, not ways a promise fails.
S3:
We recommend a facility contribution of about $115,000, on market rates of 6 November 2026, the day trading froze. One Treasury fund maturing in late 2032 pays it. Laura buys it in January 2028 with part of the 2028 deposit, then buys more of it in January 2031 with half her shares, before she meets a single co-sponsor.

It's meaningful because it's $115,000 of the $450,000 she puts in, owned before she asks anyone and announced first. Practice judges a founder's gift exactly that way, by its size against her own means and its coming first, not its share of a campaign's goal (BoardSource; Kresge Foundation), and in a laboratory a leader's example raised others' giving only when they could see the leader's means (Levati et al., 2007).

It's responsible because nothing is promised before it's owned: the ten payments never lean on it, and falling shares before the move lower what she can state, never what she has stated.

Her flexibility is the other half of the shares, about $21,200 on those rates, kept for building costs that overrun, a stronger Taiwan dollar or a co-sponsor falling short. She can always state more later but never take a stated figure back, so her figure is rounded down, whatever the fund pays above it joins her flexibility, and that half stays unpromised. Co-sponsors' own practice points the same way: funders cap their grants and owners pay the overruns, as in Taiwan's own programme for venues.

C1: We know Treasury bonds (including this one – maturing 2037) won't create wealth, but they will remove uncertainty, through duration-matching. In other words, we take Laura's requested 'high degree of certainty' to mean a near-ironclad guarantee, and we provide exactly that. Every year the bonds sit untouched is a good year – one less year of Laura's money being exposed to anything the restless markets might decide to do. Notably – Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars, so a nominal Treasury matches the liability perfectly, meaning we don't need TIPS, which would hedge against a nonexistent inflation risk.
C2: Some years, WInS lists no Treasuries maturing – so we purchased iShares iBonds (like IBTM for 2032) instead. Defined-maturity, investment-grade, liquid, cheap and transparent about yields, these behave a lot like bonds when held to their end – so we'll simply ignore price noise in the interim. Together, our T-Bonds and iBonds ensure each of Laura's payments rests on a dedicated instrument (not merely a forecast). The catch is, their terminal payout is a net asset value, as opposed to a promise of par – but in return we gain a level of liquidity which no odd-lot bond offers.
C3: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline. This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan). The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?
X1: Pension funds cover fixed payments either by matching their bonds' average life to the payments and rebalancing as rates move, or by buying one bond per payment and holding it. We do the second, which needs no forecast or trading. In January 2027, her first $300,000 buys a ladder of Treasury bonds and Treasury funds with fixed end dates, each maturing just before a January payment. A Treasury held to maturity pays exactly what it promised, whatever markets do, so no payment depends on shares.
X2:
In 2031, Laura gives co-sponsors a range. The bottom is the floor, rounded down: money she already owns. The top adds half her shares, which move into Treasuries before she names it, because a number said aloud can't quietly be halved after a bad year. The other half stays hers and liquid, as a cushion if the building costs more in Taiwan dollars.

The ladder's one weakness is that it counts on reinvesting its bonds' interest; if rates fall and stay low, it can fall short. Before Laura names her range, we price that shortfall at the day's rates, add a margin, and move that much from her kept shares into Treasuries. Her spare money shrinks before her promise does, and if it can't cover the gap, the whole range comes down.
